summary.text: An explicit telescoping identity for the binomial summand gives a second-order recurrence for the full sequence; multiplying its associated $2\times2$ transfer matrices and eliminating intermediate states yields the recurrence for every arithmetic subsequence, with the needed coefficient polynomial obtained as an explicitly divisible upper-right matrix entry.  After division, sign alternation at consecutive half-integers forces all roots into the required interval and a reflection identity gives symmetry; suitable rescaling produces $P$, while applying the same construction at $2m$ gives an even polynomial $H(x)=Q(x^2)$ whose rescaled roots lie in $[-1,1]$, with the sign count also establishing the asserted degrees.

full_proof.text:
Fix an integer \(m\geq 1\). We shall construct the required polynomials explicitly from a transfer matrix associated with a three-term recurrence for \(a(n)\).

Throughout, if \(f\) is a polynomial, \(f(x)\) denotes its value at \(x\).

## 1. A basic recurrence for \(a(n)\)

First rewrite the coefficient definition as a finite sum. For \(n>0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
&=[x^{2n}](1+x)^n(1-x)^{-n}\\
&=\sum_{j=0}^n \binom nj\binom{3n-j-1}{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Replacing \(j\) by \(n-k\) gives
\[
 a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n s(n,k),\qquad
 s(n,k):=\binom nk\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1}.
\tag{1}
\]
We also set \(a(0)=1\), as follows directly from the coefficient definition.

Introduce the three polynomials
\[
 p(x)=5x^2-5x+1,
\]
\[
 \alpha(x)=(2x+1)(2x+2)p(x),
 \qquad
 \gamma(x)=4(55x^4-34x^2+3).
\tag{2}
\]
We claim that, for every integer \(n\geq1\),
\[
 \alpha(n)a(n+1)=\gamma(n)a(n)+\alpha(-n)a(n-1).
\tag{3}
\]
For completeness, we prove this recurrence by telescoping the summand in (1).

For \(1\leq k\leq n\), direct cancellation of factorials gives the ratios
\[
 \frac{s(n+1,k)}{s(n,k)}
 =U(n,k):=
 \frac{(n+1)(2n+k)(2n+k+1)}{n(n+1-k)(n+1+k)},
\tag{4}
\]
\[
 \frac{s(n-1,k)}{s(n,k)}
 =D(n,k):=
 \frac{(n-1)(n^2-k^2)}{n(2n+k-1)(2n+k-2)},
\tag{5}
\]
and, for \(0\leq k<n\),
\[
 \frac{s(n,k+1)}{s(n,k)}
 =K(n,k):=
 \frac{(2n+k)(n-k)}{(k+1)(n+k+1)}.
\tag{6}
\]
All these identities follow immediately from
\[
 s(n,k)=\frac{n(2n+k-1)!}{k!(n-k)!(n+k)!},
\tag{7}
\]
valid for \(1\leq n\) and \(0\leq k\leq n\).

Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A(n)&=110n^5+30n^4-68n^3-20n^2+6n+2,\\
 B(n)&=410n^6-260n^5-258n^4+150n^3+30n^2-10n-2,\\
 C(n)&=290n^6-265n^5-187n^4+138n^3+33n^2-5n-4,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
 R(n,k)=A(n)k^2+B(n)k+nC(n).
\]
Put
\[
 \rho(n,k)=
 \frac{(k/n)R(n,k)}{(k-n-1)(k+2n-2)(k+2n-1)}.
\tag{8}
\]
A direct expansion after clearing denominators gives, for \(n\geq2\) and \(0\leq k<n\),
\[
 \alpha(n)U(n,k)-\alpha(-n)D(n,k)-\gamma(n)
 =K(n,k)\rho(n,k+1)-\rho(n,k).
\tag{9}
\]
This is a polynomial identity in \(n,k\): after multiplication by the displayed denominators, both sides expand to the same polynomial. Thus no analytic or convergence issue is involved.

For \(1\leq k<n\), multiplying (9) by \(s(n,k)\) and using (4)–(6) yields
\[
 \alpha(n)s(n+1,k)-\alpha(-n)s(n-1,k)-\gamma(n)s(n,k)
 =G(n,k+1)-G(n,k),
\tag{10}
\]
where, in the interior, \(G(n,k)=\rho(n,k)s(n,k)\). The same formula at \(k=0\) follows by taking \(G(n,0)=0\); here \(\rho(n,0)=0\), and the factorial-ratio identities remain valid.

At the upper boundary it is best to combine the terms \(k=n\) and \(k=n+1\), because \(s(n-1,k)=0\) for both of these indices and \(s(n,n+1)=0\). Set \(G(n,n+2)=0\), and define \(G(n,n+1)\) by the factorial expression obtained by continuing the telescoping certificate:
\[
 G(n,n+1)=
 -\frac{R(n,n+1)(3n-2)!}{n!(2n+1)!}.
\tag{11}
\]
Direct cancellation of factorials, together with the elementary rational identity
\[
 \alpha(n)u(1+v)-\gamma(n)=-\rho(n,n),
\tag{12}
\]
where
\[
 u=\frac{(n+1)(3n)(3n+1)}{n\cdot1\cdot(2n+1)},
 \qquad
 v=\frac{(3n+2)\cdot1}{(n+1)(2n+2)},
\]
shows that the sum of the left sides of (10) for \(k=n,n+1\) equals
\[
 (G(n,n+1)-G(n,n))+(G(n,n+2)-G(n,n+1)).
\]
Identity (12), like (9), is obtained simply by substituting the displayed formulas and clearing denominators.

Consequently, summing over \(k=0,\ldots,n+1\) telescopes from \(G(n,0)=0\) to \(G(n,n+2)=0\). Since \(s(r,k)=0\) for \(k>r\), the three sums that remain are exactly \(a(n+1),a(n),a(n-1)\). This proves (3) for \(n\geq2\). For \(n=1\), direct use of \(a(0)=1,a(1)=2,a(2)=16\) gives the same identity. Thus (3) holds for every \(n\geq1\).

## 2. Transfer polynomials

We now work in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb R[X]\). Define
\[
 \pi(u)=u^2-u+\frac15,
\qquad p(u)=5\pi(u),
\]
\[
 \alpha(u)=(2u+1)(2u+2)p(u),
\qquad \gamma(u)=4(55u^4-34u^2+3),
\]
and the polynomial matrix
\[
 T(u)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \gamma(u)&\alpha(-u)\\
 \alpha(u)&0
 \end{pmatrix}.
\tag{13}
\]
For \(j\geq0\), put
\[
 M_j(X)=T(X-1)T(X-2)\cdots T(X-j),
\qquad M_0=I,
\tag{14}
\]
and let \(B_j(X)\) be the upper-right entry of \(M_j(X)\).

Define the monic polynomial
\[
 E_j(X)= igl(X-(j+1)\bigr)
 \bigl(X-(j+\tfrac12)\bigr)
 \prod_{r=1}^{j-1}\pi(X-r).
\tag{15}
\]
(The product is empty when \(j=0\) or \(j=1\).) We next show that \(E_j\mid B_j\), and define
\[
 F_j(X)=\frac{B_j(X)}{E_j(X)}.
\tag{16}
\]

The key divisibility is local. Every entry of \(T(u)T(u-1)\) is divisible by \(\pi(u)\). To see this explicitly, let
\[
\begin{aligned}
 q_0(u)&=2440u^6-7320u^5+3813u^4+4574u^3-3112u^2-395u+288,\\
 q_1(u)&=55u^4-34u^2+3,\\
 q_2(u)&=55u^4-220u^3+296u^2-152u+24.
\end{aligned}
\]
Expansion gives the four entries as
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
4p(u)q_0(u)&8(u-2)(2u-3)p(u)q_1(u)\\
8(u+1)(2u+1)p(u)q_2(u)&
4(u-2)(u+1)(2u-3)(2u+1)p(u)^2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and \(p(u)=5\pi(u)\).

Moreover, the shifted quadratics \(\pi(X-r)\), for distinct integers \(r\), are relatively prime. Indeed, the roots of \(\pi(X-r)\) are
\[
 r+\frac{1-1/\sqrt5}{2},
 \qquad
 r+\frac{1+1/\sqrt5}{2},
\]
both strictly between \(r\) and \(r+1\), so quadratics belonging to distinct integer intervals have no common root. Applying the local divisibility to each adjacent pair in (14), and using this coprimality, shows that
\[
 \prod_{r=1}^{j-1}\pi(X-r)
\]
divides every entry of \(M_j\).

The remaining two linear factors in (15) arise from the final multiplication. The elementary factorization
\[
 \alpha\bigl(-(X-(n+1))\bigr)
 =20\bigl(X-(n+2)\bigr)
      \bigl(X-(n+\tfrac32)\bigr)\pi(X-n)
\tag{17}
\]
shows inductively that \((X-(j+1))(X-(j+\tfrac12))\) supplies the two remaining factors of \(B_j\). Combining this with the preceding product divisibility proves \(E_j\mid B_j\), hence (16) is a polynomial identity
\[
 E_jF_j=B_j.
\tag{18}
\]

Every entry of each factor \(T(X-r)\) has degree at most \(4\), so every entry of \(M_j\) has degree at most \(4j\). On the other hand, \(E_j\) is monic of degree \(2j\). Therefore
\[
 \deg F_j\leq 2j.
\tag{19}
\]

## 3. Alternating signs and the roots of \(F_j\)

For real \(x\), write
\[
 \tau(x)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \gamma(x)&\alpha(-x)\\
 \alpha(x)&0
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Evaluation of (14) gives
\[
 M_j(x)=\tau(x-1)\tau(x-2)\cdots\tau(x-j).
\tag{20}
\]
We need the signs of the upper-right entry at integers and half-integers.

The following elementary sign facts follow from (2):

* \(p(x)>0\) for \(x\leq0\) and for \(x\geq1\);
* \(\alpha(x)>0\) for \(x\geq1\) and for \(x\leq-3/2\);
* \(\gamma(x)>0\) whenever \(|x|\geq1\).

Thus all three nonzero entries of \(\tau(x)\) are positive for \(|x|\geq3/2\). At the two exceptional half-integers, direct substitution gives the sign patterns
\[
 \tau(-\tfrac12)=
 \begin{pmatrix}-&-\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \tau(\tfrac12)=
 \begin{pmatrix}-&0\\-&0\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{21}
\]
Multiplication of matrices with these sign patterns gives the following. A product of matrices whose three relevant entries are positive again has all entries positive (after the first two factors). Multiplying a negative column as in the second matrix of (21) by a negative row as in the first gives a strictly positive matrix. Positive factors on either side preserve the relevant strict signs. It follows from (20) that, for \(1\leq j\) and odd \(k\leq2j\),
\[
 B_j(k/2)<0\quad\text{if }k=1,
 \qquad
 B_j(k/2)>0\quad\text{if }k>1.
\tag{22}
\]

At an integer \(r\), every matrix in (20) has nonnegative entries, because \(\alpha(z)\geq0\) and \(\gamma(z)>0\) at integral \(z\). Inductively the upper-left entry of every initial product is strictly positive. In the final factor contributing to the upper-right entry, the relevant value of \(\alpha\) is strictly positive. Hence, for every even \(k\leq2j\),
\[
 B_j(k/2)>0.
\tag{23}
\]

We compare these signs with those of \(E_j\). Put
\[
 \varpi(x)=x^2-x+\frac15.
\]
Then \(\varpi(z)>0\) for every integer \(z\), while
\(
\varpi(1/2)=-1/20<0.
\)
More generally, \(\varpi(z+1/2)>0\) for every nonzero integer \(z\). From (15) it follows that
\[
 E_j(k/2)>0\quad(k\text{ even},\ 0\leq k\leq2j),
\tag{24}
\]
that \(E_j(1/2)>0\), and that
\[
 E_j(k/2)<0\quad(k\text{ odd},\ 3\leq k\leq2j).
\tag{25}
\]
Using \(B_j=E_jF_j\), equations (22)–(25) give
\[
 F_j(k/2)>0\quad(k\text{ even}),
 \qquad
 F_j(k/2)<0\quad(k\text{ odd}),
\tag{26}
\]
for every \(0\leq k\leq2j\). Thus the sign alternates at consecutive half-integers.

By the intermediate value theorem, \(F_j\) has a root in each of the \(2j\) disjoint intervals
\[
 (0,\tfrac12),(\tfrac12,1),\ldots,
 (j-\tfrac12,j).
\tag{27}
\]
These are \(2j\) distinct real roots. Together with the upper degree bound (19), this proves
\[
 \deg F_j=2j,
\tag{28}
\]
and proves that all roots of \(F_j\), including multiplicities, are real and belong to \([0,j]\). Indeed, a nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(2j\) cannot have more than \(2j\) distinct roots, so the roots in (27) exhaust all of them.

## 4. Reflection symmetry

We next prove
\[
 F_j(x)=F_j(j-x).
\tag{29}
\]
Let \(R_j(x)=\tau(x-1)\cdots\tau(x-j)\), the real evaluation of \(M_j\). Since
\[
 \tau(-x)=\tau(x)^{\mathsf T},
\tag{30}
\]
reversing the product gives
\[
 R_j(j-x)=R_j(x+1)^{\mathsf T}.
\tag{31}
\]
The products also satisfy the overlap identity
\[
 \tau(x)R_j(x)=R_j(x+1)\tau(x-j),
\tag{32}
\]
because both sides are the same ordered product of \(j+1\) consecutive transfer matrices. Taking the appropriate entries in (31) and (32) gives
\[
 \alpha(x)B_j(x)=\alpha(j-x)B_j(j-x).
\tag{33}
\]

The same weighted reflection holds for \(E_j\):
\[
 \alpha(x)E_j(x)=\alpha(j-x)E_j(j-x).
\tag{34}
\]
One direct way to check (34) is to use
\(
\varpi(1-x)=\varpi(x)
\)
and reverse the product in (15). Equivalently, after including the two linear factors from \(\alpha(x)=20(x+1/2)(x+1)\varpi(x)\), both sides become
\[
20(x+\tfrac12)(x+1)(x-j-1)(x-j-\tfrac12)
 \prod_{r=0}^{j-1}\varpi(x-r),
\]
with the factors merely written in reverse order.

Substituting \(B_j=E_jF_j\) into (33), and then using (34), gives
\[
 \alpha(x)E_j(x)F_j(x)=\alpha(x)E_j(x)F_j(j-x).
\]
As a polynomial identity, cancellation is legitimate because \(\alpha E_j\neq0\). This proves (29).

## 5. Construction of \(P\) and \(Q\)

Define
\[
 P_m(X)=F_m(mX).
\tag{35}
\]
By (28), \(P_m\) has degree \(2m\). By (29),
\[
 P_m(1-x)=F_m(m-mx)=F_m(mx)=P_m(x).
\tag{36}
\]
Every zero \(z\) of \(P_m\) satisfies \(mz\) is a zero of \(F_m\). Since \(m>0\) and all zeros of \(F_m\) are real and in \([0,m]\), all zeros of \(P_m\) are real and in \([0,1]\).

For the second polynomial, first define
\[
 H_m(X)=5^{-m}F_{2m}\bigl(m(X+1)\bigr).
\tag{37}
\]
It has degree \(4m\). Reflection symmetry (29), now with \(j=2m\), gives
\[
 H_m(-x)=5^{-m}F_{2m}(m(1-x))
 =5^{-m}F_{2m}(2m-m(1-x))
 =H_m(x).
\]
Thus \(H_m\) is even, so every odd coefficient vanishes. There is therefore a unique polynomial \(Q_m\in\mathbb R[X]\) such that
\[
 H_m(X)=Q_m(X^2).
\tag{38}
\]
Since \(\deg H_m=4m\), we have \(\deg Q_m=2m\).

If \(z\in\mathbb C\) satisfies \(Q_m(z^2)=0\), then by (38), \(H_m(z)=0\), and hence
\[
 F_{2m}(m(z+1))=0.
\]
All roots of \(F_{2m}\) are real and in \([0,2m]\). Since \(m>0\), it follows that \(z\) is real and
\[
 0\leq m(z+1)\leq2m,
\]
that is,
\[
 -1\leq z\leq1.
\tag{39}
\]
This proves the required zero property for \(Q_m(X^2)\).

It remains only to prove the desired recurrence.

## 6. Passing from the basic recurrence to the \(m\)-step recurrence

Let \(u(0),u(1),\ldots\) be any real sequence satisfying (3). Define the state vector
\[
 v_n=\binom{u(n)}{u(n-1)}
\]
for \(n\geq1\). At \(n=0\), one may define the second component as \(u(1)-6u(0)\); this makes the same matrix relation valid because \(\alpha(0)=2\) and \(\gamma(0)=12\). Equation (3) is equivalent to
\[
 \alpha(n)v_{n+1}=\tau(n)v_n.
\tag{40}
\]
For integers \(t,j\geq0\), let
\[
 d(t,j)=\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\alpha(t+i).
\tag{41}
\]
Iterating (40) gives
\[
 d(t,j)v_{t+j}=R_j(t+j)v_t.
\tag{42}
\]

Set
\[
 r=mn,
 \qquad t_-=m(n-1),
 \qquad L=R_m(r),
 \qquad U=R_m(r+m).
\]
Applying (42) over the lower and upper blocks gives
\[
 d(t_-,m)v_r=L v_{t_-},
 \qquad
 d(r,m)v_{r+m}=U v_r.
\tag{43}
\]
Eliminate the second components of these two vector equations. A direct two-by-two determinant calculation yields
\[
 L_{01}d(t_-,m)d(r,m)u(r+m)
 +U_{01}\det(L)u(t_-)
 =d(t_-,m)(UL)_{01}u(r).
\tag{44}
\]
Because adjoining the two blocks produces the length-\(2m\) product, \((UL)_{01}=B_{2m}(r+m)\), while
\[
 L_{01}=B_m(r),\qquad U_{01}=B_m(r+m).
\tag{45}
\]

We now factor every coefficient in (44). Define
\[
 \Omega_+(m,r)=\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2r+k),
 \qquad
 \Omega_-(m,r)=\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2r-k).
\tag{46}
\]
Since
\[
 \alpha(x)=5(2x+1)(2x+2)\varpi(x),
\tag{47}
\]
pairing the consecutive linear factors gives
\[
 d(r,m)=5^m\Omega_+(m,r)
 \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\varpi(r+i).
\tag{48}
\]
Also, from (15),
\[
 E_j(x)=(x-j-1)(x-j-\tfrac12)
 \prod_{i=0}^{j-2}\varpi(x-i-1).
\tag{49}
\]
Splitting the quadratic product in (49) into two consecutive blocks gives
\[
 E_{2m}(r+m)=E_m(r)
 \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\varpi(r+i).
\tag{50}
\]

The determinant of one transfer matrix is
\[
 \det\tau(x)=-\alpha(-x)\alpha(x).
\]
Therefore
\[
 \det L=(-1)^m
 \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha\bigl(-(r-i-1)\bigr)
 \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha(r-i-1).
\tag{51}
\]
The second product in (51) is \(d(r-m,m)=d(t_-,m)\), with its factors reversed. Applying (47), using \(\varpi(1-x)=\varpi(x)\), and pairing the linear factors in the first product gives the identity
\[
 E_m(r+m)
 \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\alpha\bigl(-(r-i-1)\bigr)
 =5^mE_{2m}(r+m)\Omega_-(m,r).
\tag{52}
\]
This follows directly by comparing factors: the quadratic factors combine according to (49), while the linear factors are exactly \(2r-1,2r-2,\ldots,2r-2m\).

Use now \(B_j=E_jF_j\), (35), and (38). Since \(r=mn\),
\[
 F_m(r)=P_m(n),
 \qquad
 F_m(-r)=P_m(-n),
\tag{53}
\]
and reflection (29) gives
\[
 F_m(r+m)=F_m(-r).
\tag{54}
\]
Also, from (37)–(38),
\[
 F_{2m}(r+m)=5^mQ_m(n^2).
\tag{55}
\]

Substituting (45), (48), (50), (52), and (53)–(55) into (44), all three terms have the common factor
\[
 K=5^m d(t_-,m)E_{2m}(r+m).
\]
Except when \((m,n)=(1,2)\), this factor is nonzero. Indeed, every factor of \(d(t_-,m)\) is positive at a nonnegative integer, and (49) shows that the only possible zero of \(E_{2m}(r+m)\) in the present range comes from
\(r+m-(2m)-1=0\), namely \(m(n-1)=1\), which is exactly \((m,n)=(1,2)\); the other linear factor cannot vanish at these integer parameters, and all remaining \(\varpi\)-factors are positive at the relevant integers.

Cancelling \(K\) in the nonexceptional cases gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Omega_+(m,mn)P_m(n)u(m(n+1))\\
&\quad+(-1)^m\Omega_-(m,mn)P_m(-n)u(m(n-1))
=Q_m(n^2)u(mn).
\end{aligned}
\tag{56}
\]

For the exceptional pair \((m,n)=(1,2)\), direct multiplication in the definitions gives
\[
 F_1(X)=4p(X),
\]
\[
 F_2(X)=80(55X^4-220X^3+296X^2-152X+24).
\]
Substitution into (35), (37), and (38) reduces (56) exactly to the basic recurrence (3) at index \(2\). Hence (56) holds in the exceptional case as well.

Finally take \(u(n)=a(n)\), which satisfies (3) by Section 1, and write \(b(n)=a(mn)\). Since
\[
 \Omega_+(m,mn)=\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn+k),
 \qquad
 \Omega_-(m,mn)=\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn-k),
\]
equation (56) is precisely
\[
\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn+k)\right)P_m(n)b(n+1)
+(-1)^m\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2m}(2mn-k)\right)P_m(-n)b(n-1)
=Q_m(n^2)b(n)
\]
for every \(n\geq1\).

The polynomials \(P=P_m\) and \(Q=Q_m\) have degree \(2m\); equation (36) gives \(P(x)=P(1-x)\); all zeros of \(P\) are real and lie in \([0,1]\); and (39) shows that every zero of \(Q(x^2)\) is real and lies in \([-1,1]\). This proves all parts of the conjecture.
